doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Guitar parts in 1950s sessions and overdubbing
summary: Guitar parts were never written out, only changes; leads were improvised and sometimes redone or overdubbed into guitar sections.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Any other particular studio dates like that stick in your mind, people that you’ve recorded for?

Oh there were so many. But the strings really get to me. That I have to say, that’s great. And the other things of course with Keith and a lot of doowop type things, a lot of that where you’re recording sessions, you just go in and play. And of course they couldn’t write for guitar in those days, all they did was write the change and then if they wanted you to play a lead — maybe someone told you this — like in the fifties they never wrote for guitar, they just wrote the changes and they would say okay, take a lead here between these four measures and you’d have to change it and you’d play your own, what you wanted to play. And now they’re writing for guitar.
Oh they’re writing out the solo parts?
Well they have been in the past say ten years. But they never did write the actual single notes out for guitar.
Did they get specific enough to say like let’s do that again because we didn’t like that lead you played?
But you’d have to do the whole rhythm section probably, or did you do any overdubbing of just solo parts?
Yes, but not on any big recordings I mean I’m trying to think of now, where I did like three parts. I generally did like three, four parts where it sounded more like a guitar section.
Yeah. Three guitars. They can’t all do the same thing, right?
